It’s the Moscow summit that has the whole world talking.

   CIA Director John Ratcliffe  flew to the Russian capital this week to meet with his Russian counterpart. This type of rare spy-vs-spy summit tends to only happen when there is really sensitive stuff to discuss.

   Can Ratcliffe reassert U.S. power in this relationship, something other U.S. officials have failed to do? Will Russia listen to U.S. warnings?

   There’s a reason many are nervous. At least one armed Russian drone has been found at a German airport , suggesting Moscow is looking to expand its military tactics beyond Ukraine.

   Ratcliffe is one of the most fascinating people in the Trump administration’s national security team. Often operating in the shadows (fair enough, he is the CIA director), his Russia visit came three months after he turned up in Havana, another focus of spying and subterfuge.

   President Trump has a large and unconventional national security team, full of people with both official and unofficial roles. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had earlier played interlocutor roles with Russia, but Ratcliffe’s visit makes it seem like the White House might be changing its approach after more than a year of dead ends.

   Trump has long hailed his good relationship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin as being key to helping resolve differences, but Putin has so far refused to back away from the Ukraine war. Even the brief Alaska summit last year between Trump and Putin, which had a military flyover, led to no change.

   Time keeps ticking, and the U.S.’s European allies remain anxious about what Russia might do next. Some senior European officials have alleged that Russia is probing NATO defenses, and U.S. intelligence has found that Russia could test NATO’s resolve even further. Trump on Thursday said that Putin wouldn’t attack a NATO country.

   What will Putin’s next move be, and how might the U.S. respond?

CIA Chief’s Trip to Moscow Has Everyone On Edge
 
Plus, companies that cut checks for Trump begin to worry, and efforts to prosecute Anthony Fauci fall apart
 
 
ALEX BRANDON/AP
 

Good morning. It’s the Moscow summit that has the whole world talking.

 

CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to the Russian capital this week to meet with his Russian counterpart. This type of rare spy-vs-spy summit tends to only happen when there is really sensitive stuff to discuss.

 

Can Ratcliffe reassert U.S. power in this relationship, something other U.S. officials have failed to do? Will Russia listen to U.S. warnings?

 

There’s a reason many are nervous. At least one armed Russian drone has been found at a German airport, suggesting Moscow is looking to expand its military tactics beyond Ukraine.

 

Ratcliffe is one of the most fascinating people in the Trump administration’s national security team. Often operating in the shadows (fair enough, he is the CIA director), his Russia visit came three months after he turned up in Havana, another focus of spying and subterfuge.

 

President Trump has a large and unconventional national security team, full of people with both official and unofficial roles. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had earlier played interlocutor roles with Russia, but Ratcliffe’s visit makes it seem like the White House might be changing its approach after more than a year of dead ends.

 

Trump has long hailed his good relationship with Russian leader Vladimir Putin as being key to helping resolve differences, but Putin has so far refused to back away from the Ukraine war. Even the brief Alaska summit last year between Trump and Putin, which had a military flyover, led to no change.

 

Time keeps ticking, and the U.S.’s European allies remain anxious about what Russia might do next. Some senior European officials have alleged that Russia is probing NATO defenses, and U.S. intelligence has found that Russia could test NATO’s resolve even further. Trump on Thursday said that Putin wouldn’t attack a NATO country.

 

What will Putin’s next move be, and how might the U.S. respond?

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Anthropic: A federal judge ruled Thursday that the Trump administration violated the artificial-intelligence company’s First Amendment rights by blacklisting it as a supply-chain risk.

 

Abdul El-Sayed: Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate is taking steps to connect with voters beyond the progressive base.

 

Lake Ontario: Trump signed an executive order on Thursday renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America while the trade conflict with Canada escalates.

 

Chuck Edwards: The Republican congressman from North Carolina has defended sending poetry and gifts to two young staffers after sexual-harassment allegations.

 

Trump’s Friday: This morning in Houston the president will award Artemis II crew members with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor, then at noon will call the International Space Station.

What I’m Following

 
 
ALLISON ROBBERT/AP
 

A federal judge has temporarily blocked Trump’s mail-in ballot rules. The judge issued a temporary restraining order Thursday that stops the government from carrying out new U.S. Postal Service regulations days before the first ballots are due to go out in some parts of the country.

 

GOP attempts to prosecute Anthony Fauci are coming undone. Senate Republicans’ effort to hold Fauci in contempt has stalled in part because Trump isn’t eager to do so. And some administration officials are skeptical that the current legal approach is procedurally sound enough to indict the retired public-health official.

 

Companies that wrote big checks to Trump are now worrying Democrats will investigate them. Tech firms are starting to privately panic that they’ll face a wave of subpoenas if Democrats retake control of the House. Some companies are writing big checks for Democrats ahead of the midterms and creating internal task forces to game out responses to potential congressional inquiries.
